This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
 - $500
Is there $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that\[\lim_{n\to \infty}\frac{1_A\ast 1_A(n)}{\log n}\]exists and is $\neq 0$?
#66: [Er56][Er59][Er80,p.98][ErGr80][Er85c][Er89d][Er90][Er95][Er97c][Er97f][Va99,1.16]
number theory | 
additive basis
A suitably constructed random set has this property if we are allowed to ignore an exceptional set of density zero. The challenge is obtaining this with no exceptional set. Erdős believed the answer should be no. In [Er80] he explicitly asked whether there exists such a set where the limit is $1$ (and did not believe there existed such a sequence).
Erdős and Sárközy proved that\[\frac{\lvert 1_A\ast 1_A(n)-\log n\rvert}{\sqrt{\log n}}\to 0\]is impossible. Erdős suggests it may even be true that the $\liminf$ and $\limsup$ of $1_A\ast 1_A(n)/\log n$ are always separated by some absolute constant. 
Horváth [Ho07] proved that\[\lvert 1_A\ast 1_A(n)-\log n\rvert \leq (1-\epsilon)\sqrt{\log n}\]cannot hold for all large $n$.
Additional thanks to: Boris Alexeev and Mark Sellke

 A recent preprint by Christian Táfula, "Representation functions with prescribed rates of growth" (arXiv:2405.01530, last revised May 2026), provides new insights right at the logarithmic boundary:
1. Above the boundary: The paper proves that if $F(n)$ is a regularly varying function satisfying $\lim_{n \to \infty} F(n)/\log n = \infty$, then there exists a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that $1_A * 1_A(n) \sim F(n)$. This establishes that any rate of growth strictly faster than $\log n$ is attainable.
2. The logarithmic sparsity wall: The paper presents a probabilistic heuristic indicating that if $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ satisfies 
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{1_A * 1_A(n)}{\log n} < 1,$$ 
then $1_A * 1_A(n) = 0$ for infinitely many $n$. 
Since a limit $\lim_{n \to \infty} (1_A * 1_A(n))/\log n = c > 0$ requires the representation function to be positive for all sufficiently large $n$, this heuristic strongly implies that no such limit can exist for any constant $c < 1$.

 The best progress on this problem seems to be by (G. Horváth, "An improvement of a theorem of Erdős and Sárközy", Pollack Periodica 2 (2007, Supp. 1), 155–164) which shows that $|1_A*1_A(n)-\log(n)|\leq (1-\epsilon)\sqrt{\log n})$ cannot hold simultaneously for all sufficiently large $n$. Horváth also shows the same result for all higher self- convolutions $1_A*1_A*\dots*1_A$.
